prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Whose sense in so evil consort, their stepdame Nature lays, That ravishing delight in them most sweet tunes do not raise; Or if they do delight therein, yet are so cloyed with wit, As with sententious lips to set a title vain on it: O let them hear these sacred tunes, and learn in wonder’s schools, To be (in things past bounds of wit) fools, if they be not fools. Who have so leaden eyes, as not to see sweet beauty’s show, Or seeing, have so wooden wits, as not that worth to know; Or knowing, have so muddy minds, as not to be in love; Or loving, have so frothy thoughts, as eas’ly thence to move: Or let them see these heavenly beams, and in fair letters read A lesson fit, both sight and skill, love and firm love to breed. Hear then, but then with wonder hear; see but adoring see, No mortal gifts, no earthly fruits, now here descended be; See, do you see this face? a face? nay, image of the skies, Of which the two life-giving lights are figured in her eyes: Hear you this soul-invading voice, and count it but a voice? The very essence of their tunes, when Angels do rejoice.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Whose, Nature, That

outputs.L1:
Those whose senses their stepmother Nature has cast in so discordant a mold that the sweetest melodies awaken in them no rapturous delight—or who, though delighted, are so surfeited with wit that they dismiss such music with hollow judgments—let them hear these sacred strains and learn in wonder’s school to become fools in matters beyond the bounds of reason, if fools they are not already.

Those whose eyes are too leaden to behold the spectacle of sweet beauty; or who, beholding it, have minds too wooden to recognize its worth; or who, recognizing it, have souls too clouded to fall in love; or who, loving, have thoughts too fickle to remain steadfast—let them gaze upon these heavenly beams and read, inscribed in fair letters, a lesson capable of nurturing sight and understanding, love and enduring devotion.

Listen, then—but listen in wonder. Look—but look in adoration. No mortal gifts, no earthly fruits, have descended here. Do you see this face? A face? No: it is an image of the heavens, whose two life-giving lights are reflected in her eyes. Do you hear this soul-invading voice and count it merely a voice? It is the very essence of the harmonies sung when angels rejoice.
outputs.L2:
Those whom harsh stepmother Nature has endowed with such corrupted judgment  
That the loveliest music awakens in them no transporting joy—or, if it does,  
Whose intellect is so overfed that they dismiss it with pompous phrases  
And give its beauty some empty, pretentious name—  
Let them listen to these holy harmonies and study in the school of wonder,  
Learning to become fools before what lies beyond reason, unless fools they already are.

Those whose heavy eyes cannot perceive the display of exquisite beauty;  
Or who perceive it, yet lack the understanding to recognize its value;  
Or who know its worth, yet possess hearts too dull to fall in love;  
Or who love, but are so fickle that their affection quickly fades—  
Let them behold these celestial rays and read, written in beauty itself,  
A lesson capable of awakening sight and judgment, love and steadfast devotion.

Listen, then—but listen in amazement; look—but look with reverence:  
What has descended here is no mortal talent, no product of the earth.  
Do you see this countenance? Can it be called merely a face? No—it mirrors heaven,  
And its two life-bestowing stars are represented in her eyes.  
Do you hear this voice that enters and possesses the soul, and think it only a voice?  
It is the very substance of the music sounded by rejoicing angels.
outputs.L3:
Those who cannot take delight in sweet music are portrayed as lacking a natural sensitivity to beauty, or as being so constrained by intellect that they cannot surrender themselves to wonder. Sacred music, by contrast, teaches its listeners to recognize that reason has limits and that some truths must be approached through reverence, awe, and emotional openness.

Within this framework, the proper appreciation of beauty follows a spiritual progression: one first sees beauty, then comes to understand its significance, grows to love it, and finally remains steadfastly devoted to it. The woman’s beauty and voice inspire precisely this response because they are presented not as ordinary mortal qualities, but as gifts of heavenly origin. Her face is likened to the sky, while her eyes resemble radiant, life-giving lights. Her voice, meanwhile, is compared to the joyful harmony of angels. Together, these images elevate her beyond the earthly realm, suggesting that her presence offers a glimpse of divine beauty and calls forth wonder, love, and faithful devotion.
outputs.L4:
Those whose hearts have never been stirred by music, and whose eyes have remained indifferent to beauty, should pause before her in reverent silence. Let them listen to her voice and gaze upon her face without trying to reduce their wonder to argument or explanation. Such grace is not meant to be measured by ordinary judgment; it must be received humbly, as one receives a mystery.

For her countenance seems illuminated by something more than earthly loveliness, and her voice carries an echo of heaven. Together they awaken the senses, enlighten the understanding, and move the heart toward a love that neither time nor reason can overthrow. In her presence, perception becomes revelation, thought gives way to awe, and affection rises beyond mortal comprehension into steadfast devotion.
outputs.L5:
**Whose Nature Is That?**

Whose voice is that in the whispering trees?  
Whose shadow moves beneath the moon?  
Nature answers through rustling leaves,  
the song of a river, and flowers in bloom.

That beauty belongs to no one alone.  
It is shared by every creature on Earth.  
Nature is our home, our teacher, and our responsibility—a gift whose value is beyond measure.
